title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
body:
Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work.
The scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems.
NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, [$250 million compute commitment](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-commits-250-million-to-advance-uk-agentic-safety-and-security-research-over-the-next-five-years) to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research.
NVIDIA’s Investments in the UK
NVIDIA has been investing in the U.K. startup ecosystem, supporting companies including Basecamp Research, Ineffable Intelligence, Synthesia, Wayve and many more.
Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Boltz, Foresight, Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane.
Boltz, a London-based AI startup founded by MIT researchers, builds biomolecular models and AI agents that help scientists predict molecular structures and interactions, and design potential new medicines.
Foresight, a London-based startup, helps owners of major infrastructure projects, including hyperscale data centers, predict completion dates, mitigate risks and accelerate time to revenue.
Hiverge, a Cambridge-based AI startup founded by researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Cambridge, builds an AI discovery engine that automatically writes and optimizes algorithms for tasks such as faster AI training and complex logistics planning.
Prima Mente, a London-based AI biology startup, focuses on building biological foundation models to decode complex diseases and identify novel therapeutic targets, starting with Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and ALS.
Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum computing startup, builds real-time error correction hardware and software that work across all major qubit types, helping quantum computers become reliable enough for practical use.
In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the [Earthshot Prize](https://earthshotprize.org/news/the-earthshot-prize-teams-up-with-nvidia/), joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges.
Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK
In energy, [Fuse Energy](http://fuseenergy.com/blog) is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households.
Meanwhile, sovereign AI company [Locai Labs](https://www.locailabs.com/news/nvidia-nemotron-personas-uk) released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems.
Healthcare
In healthcare, [OneAdvanced](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261014126036/en/OneAdvanced-Leverages-NVIDIA-Technologies-to-Advance-Safer-Agentic-AI-for-UK-Critical-Sectors) is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients.
Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence.
[Speechmatics](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/10/14/3380824/0/en/voice-ai-model-built-to-accurately-capture-real-multilingual-medical-conversations.html) is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed.
[Apian](https://www.apian.health/press-releases/foundation-world-model-pathology-logistics), Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care.
[Danaher](https://investors.danaher.com/2026-10-14-Danaher-Collaborates-with-NVIDIA-to-Advance-Autonomous-Science?asPDF) and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback.
Smart Cities
On the civic side, [Liverpool City Region](https://www.liverpoolcityregion-ca.gov.uk/news/liverpool-city-region-regional-compute-announcement) is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a [sovereign AI](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nations-deploy-ai-strategic-priorities/) strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K.
[Digital Jersey](https://www.digital.je/), Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services.
Financial Services
In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions.
Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling.
Lloyds Banking Group built [ATUM](https://medium.com/ai-at-lloyds-banking-group/introducing-atum-a-foundation-model-for-banking-4d5291577d50), a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And [Starling](https://www.starlingbank.com/news/starling-backs-uk-sovereign-cloud/) is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure.
NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while [Modulr](http://www.modulrfinance.com/newsroom/ai-models-for-payments) is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations.
Quantum
Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift.
[Riverlane](https://www.riverlane.com/blog/riverlane-and-nvidia-explores-faster-calibration-for-qec-with-nvidia-accelerated-computing) has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems.
Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the [NVIDIA Inception program](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/?ncid=pa-srch-goog-816-prsp-txt-en-us-1-l1-top-performing&_bt=819982985676&_bk=inception%20program&_bm=e&_bn=g&_bg=201901011071&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24112104929&gbraid=0AAAAAD4XAoGsL9yDVwjilPj3lJfpbwy7w&gclid=CjwKCAjwlY3WBhANEiwApsNrLX_TzIn9wlPhGAYVpRWZZBSFd950S01PqeXFfmBTexJqI4gnTBzY9RoCEwoQAvD_BwE) for cutting-edge startups.
Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s [GTC Berlin keynote](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/gtc/keynote/) on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
body:
Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently.
Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive.
Software partners including ABA Technology, Akila, Galene AI, Honeywell Technologies, K2K, Linker Vision, Milestone, Onetera, ThinkDeep and Younite AI are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services.
Video courtesy of Linker Vision and MVRDV.
NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the [NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia/video-search-and-summarization) (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with [NVIDIA Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) libraries.
Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere.
In the U.K., the [Liverpool City Region](https://www.liverpoolcityregion-ca.gov.uk/news/liverpool-city-region-regional-compute-announcement), [K2K](https://www.k2k.ai/ikm-state-of-the-art/k2k%C2%AE-integrates-nvidia-cosmos-3-and-metropolis-vss-3-into-ikm%C2%AE-technology-to-scale-sovereign-ai-services-across-smart-spaces) is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The [Island of Jersey](https://www.digital.je/news-events/digital-news/digital-jersey-explores-responsible-ai-adoption-across-the-island-with-nvidia/) is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management.
Video courtesy of K2K.
In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or, [Akila](https://www.akila3d.com/media/cote-dor-sovereign-digital-twin-ai-agents) and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale.
Video courtesy of Akila.
In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials.
In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI, Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data.
At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges, Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce.
In the Nordics, Younite AI is developing a [digital twin experience](https://younite.ai/physical-ai-press-release-gtc-scewc26) with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival.
These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw.
Elsewhere in the region, [Honeywell Technologies](https://www.honeywell.com/us/en/news/press-releases/2026/10/honeywell-technologies-launches-forge-cognition-with-nvidia-and-dell-technologies-advancing-physical-ai-across-buildings-and-industrial-operations) is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations.
Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies.
Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities
For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents.
System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations.
Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at [Smart City Expo World Congress](https://www.smartcityexpo.com/), running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona.

title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
body:
Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
Collaborating with the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) to protect users without compromising privacy.
Scams, such as investment fraud, fake job offers, and impersonation of public officials make up over half of Singaporeâs reported crimes, and account for more than [S$4 billion in losses since 2019](https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/scam-tracker-what-are-the-trends-in-singapore-and-how-much-money-has-been-lost-in-2026). At the same time, scam tactics have shifted from simple phishing to complex social engineering, whereby attackers manipulate victims with convincing conversations before requesting money. Such scams now account for up to 80% of all losses.
To address this, Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have been working together as part of our [National AI Partnership](https://deepmind.google/blog/strengthening-singapores-ai-future-a-new-national-partnership/) with the Singapore Government. Together, we've fine-tuned a privacy-preserving, on-device scam detection model.
On-device AI protection without compromising privacy
Generic models often struggle with local deception techniques, making scam detection harder. To address this, Googleâs lightweight Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations. These ranged from impersonations of public institutions, banks, and local figures, to trending regional schemes. This ensures the fine-tuned model will be able to distinguish benign social chatter from genuine manipulation when deployed in applications installed by citizens.
Unlike traditional threat detection, which relies on server-side scanning of messages in the cloud, this model can process conversation data directly on-device. When integrated into applications, this will allow faster analysis of conversation patterns to detect manipulative intent and help citizens act before financial or credential exposure can occur.
The roll out of the model within applications will be carefully phased and developed in partnership with the Singapore Government. When deployed, the model will only be able to access on-device conversations with the user's consent, in accordance with the terms of use of that application. As the model runs entirely on-device, neither the Singapore Government nor Google, will be able to access usersâ conversations through its deployment.
Under the hood: local context and edge efficiency
When the model detects manipulative conversational patterns, it triggers a real-time warning directly on the user's device advising them to pause and exercise caution before sharing sensitive information or funds.
Running a complex scam classifier model on modern smartphones is no easy task, with battery efficiency being a critical area of concern. To do this, we're relying on a two-stage pipeline:
- Stage 1: A lightweight, efficient classifier screens inbound messages, using minimal power, focused on catching potential threats.
- Stage 2: In-context analysis with our fine-tuned Gemma model, where we analyze a larger snapshot of the conversation to confirm a threat or discard a false alarm.
Built on strict governance
Presented at Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW 2026), this collaboration provides a model for messaging platforms balancing user protection with end-to-end encryption. Strict governance was maintained throughout development:
- Sovereign Sandbox: Fine-tuning took place within GovTech Singapore's managed and maintained GCP environment, keeping training data isolated.
- No Citizen Data: Training strictly excluded private or personally identifiable information, utilising anonymised datasets derived from scam reports and intelligence feeds.
- Stress-Testing: The model was tested against synthetic dialogues and local corpora to cover diverse scam categories and evolving impersonation tactics.
The future of on-device safety
The project demonstrates how AI can help counter criminality without compromising safety or privacy. It also shows how governments and model providers can work together to build tech for public good. With this lightweight, on-device model, we've proven the ability for local, real-time scam detection while ensuring chat interactions remain secure. We look forward to sharing more soon on our collaboration with the Singapore government, as well as exploring the potential for similar technology to be deployed in other countries.

title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
body:
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
Earlier this year, we shared an [update on our election safeguards](https://www.anthropic.com/news/election-safeguards-update), which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.
Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
How people use Claude for elections and politics
Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.[1](#footnote-1)
Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to [increase](https://www.anthropic.com/news/elections-ai-2024).
This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our [election integrity policies](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.[2](#footnote-2)
Connecting people to trusted sources
Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from [Democracy Works](https://www.democracy.works/).
Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.
Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.
Measuring and preventing political bias
When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our [political evenhandedness evaluation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/political-even-handedness). Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.
As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies. [The Future of Free Speech](https://futurefreespeech.org/), an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the [Foundation for American Innovation](https://www.thefai.org/) compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The [Collective Intelligence Project](https://www.cip.org/) surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.
These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.
We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.
How we define misuse
Our [Usage Policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we [announced](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update) last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.
We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently [published a guide](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/4zrzovbb/website/027b10ca405e9bb66b98c88d911b4b21a0b70123.pdf) to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.
Testing and strengthening our defenses
We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the [Institute for Strategic Dialogue](https://www.isdglobal.org/) (ISD) and the [McCain Institute](https://www.mccaininstitute.org/), both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.
Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.
Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share [examples](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions) of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.
What we've found
Our recent [threat intelligence report](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.
Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.
Looking ahead
More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.

title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
body:
Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.
“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
Supporting responsible AI in Singapore
Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.
“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”
“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”
Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the [Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox](https://www.imda.gov.sg/resources/press-releases-factsheets-and-speeches/press-releases/2023/generative-ai-evaluation-sandbox) run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a [red-teaming project](https://www.anthropic.com/news/challenges-in-red-teaming-ai-systems) in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.
Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.
We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the [Anthropic Economic Index](https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index#global-usage), and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.
How Singapore is working with Claude
In our latest [Economic Index](https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index#country-usage), Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.
In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.
In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with [in-region inference](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-anthropic-models-on-amazon-bedrock-for-in-region-inference-in-seoul-and-singapore/) on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.
Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.
Building with the developer community
This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.
Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.
Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our [careers page](https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs?office=4063231008).

title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
body:
[content type paper](/research/)published October 2026
Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
AuthorsJie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter
Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
AuthorsJie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter
Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora.

title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
body:
Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities.

title: Agent observability on the Claude Platform
body:
Agent observability on the Claude Platform
Announcing OpenTelemetry traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs on the Claude Platform.
You can now send OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs to any OTel tool, and follow each step your agents take. If you already send Claude Code or Cowork traces to your observability tool, the agents you build on the Claude Platform can also show up in the same place.
Trace agents with OpenTelemetry
Trusting an agent with more access starts with tracing its model calls, tool use, and MCP server calls. Review its traces, then widen its access as it proves reliable.
Add a destination in the Claude Console, and every agent turn, model call, and tool use arrives in your observability tool as a standard OpenTelemetry trace, with latency, tokens, and IDs.
Works with your observability tools
Claude traces follow the [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/), so data from Claude and other providers works in the same tools and dashboards.
- Debug agents next to the rest of your stack. In
[Grafana Cloud](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/observe-and-act/agent-observability/guides/send-claude-platform-traces/),[Honeycomb](https://docs.honeycomb.io/send-data/use-cases/claude-platform),[Sentry](https://sentry.io/cookbook/trace-claude-platform-with-opentelemetry/), and[Splunk](https://agent-observability-docs.splunk.com/sdk-api/third-party-integrations/claude), agent traces sit beside your logs and metrics, so you can see which service a slow or failed step came from. - Improve agents with production data. With
[Arize AI](https://arize.com/docs/ax/integrations/platforms/claude-managed-agents/claude-managed-agents-tracing),[Braintrust](https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/integrations/ai-providers/anthropic#export-opentelemetry-traces-from-the-claude-api),[Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/instrument/otel_instrumentation/?tab=python#using-claude-managed-agents),[Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/integrations/model-providers/claude-platform),[LangSmith by LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/trace-anthropic),[New Relic](https://newrelic.com/blog/news/anthropic-otel-ai-observability), and[PostHog](https://posthog.com/docs/ai-observability/installation/anthropic?tab=Claude+Platform&utm_source=anthropic&utm_campaign=anthropic-otel), you can turn real traces into evals, catch quality issues, and measure whether a change helped. - Track usage across your organization. Send traces to
[Databricks Unity Gateway](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/unified-trace-table)so platform and security teams can see token usage by team and flag unusual activity.
Claude traces also work with any other OpenTelemetry tool that accepts a standard OTLP endpoint.
Get started
OpenTelemetry traces on the Claude Platform is available in public beta. Managed Agents and the Messages API need a destination in the Claude Console, while Claude SDKs export traces automatically.
See the [docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/opentelemetry) to get started.
“Agents that touch a company’s books have to show their work, the same way an accountant does. Our agents run on the Claude Platform and our telemetry lives in Grafana Cloud, and native OpenTelemetry export from Claude puts each model call in the same trace as the reconciliation or journal-entry workflow it ran inside. We see the prompt version, tool calls, latency, and token spend alongside the rest of our stack, so when an auditor asks what an agent did and why, we can answer from one timeline.”
“At Foxglove, we’re building agents that help robotics teams debug their robots. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform lets us analyze agent interactions in PostHog alongside product usage data. That helps us evaluate how our agents perform in practice, identify where they fall short, and prioritize improvements for robotics teams.”
“Claude powers some of Ramp’s most capable internal and customer-facing agents. We built Reflect, an agentic system that scores their Langfuse traces, finds recurring failures, and proposes fixes. On some agents, we’ve already cut token usage by 10–20% and made sessions 30% faster. But Reflect can only improve what it observes. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude API can feed high-fidelity instrumentation directly into that improvement loop, with no extra steps.”
“At Sterling Labs, we tune our systems like a race team tunes its engine. For agents analyzing live markets 24/7, Langfuse is our pit wall. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform streams every trace straight in with no custom instrumentation, so my team can focus on the edge, not the wiring.”

title: Lessons from scaling teams of coding agents: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost
body:
Agent teams are building software
In the past year, teams of coding agents have moved from interesting demos to building large-scale software projects. Sixteen Claude agents wrote a 100,000-line C compiler that can build the Linux kernel, in a project that took about 2,000 agent sessions and $20,000 in API costs [[1](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler)]. Cursor ran hundreds of agents that together wrote a web browser from scratch, more than a million lines of code, in about a week [[2](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents)]. Bun was ported from Zig to Rust in 11 days, with 64 Claude agents running in parallel at its peak [[3](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust)].
Each of these teams produced working software, but they differ from one another in many ways at once, from the models and roles to the scope of the projects themselves. The C compiler's agents worked as peers with no orchestrator and claimed tasks through lock files. Cursor used a hierarchical structure, with planners recursively decomposing work into subtasks delegated to hundreds of worker agents. Bun assigned fixed roles, giving each piece of work to one implementer, two adversarial reviewers, and one fixer.
Comparing them, however, says little about which design choices mattered or what they cost compared to a single agent. Factory's study of their own multi-agent system, which cycles an orchestrator, an implementer, and a validator in a fixed loop, shows how large that cost can be [[4](https://factory.com/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks)]. On one task, rebuilding the geospatial library GDAL, their three-role team more than doubled the reward achieved by a single agent, nearly reaching behavioral parity with the reference program, but cost 14 times as much and took 13 times as long.
So agent teams can do more than a single agent, but they cost more to run and usually take longer. This raises an important question: if a team of agents is a new way to spend inference compute, how should it be organized to be both effective and efficient? To answer it, we built a controlled testbed and ran teams of coding agents on it.
Figure 1. An illustrative run of a coding-agent team. A lead hands out work to its workers, who explore the original program, write code, and check it in a shared workspace.
A controlled testbed
A minimal harness
We built a deliberately minimal harness, inspired by [mini-SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent) [[5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793)], so that we could change one design choice at a time. Every agent works through a simple bash
tool, in one workspace shared by the whole team. One agent, the lead, receives the task and hands out work with a delegate_agent
tool. A worker sees only the subtask it is given and reports back when it is done. Given the task, the lead dynamically decides how many workers to spawn, what each one does, and how to consolidate what they return.1
Each delegate_agent
call either starts a new worker with a fresh context window or resumes a worker the lead has used before. A resumed worker keeps its prior context, so the lead can follow up with an agent that already knows part of the program. For example, the lead can ask a worker to fix the bugs in the code it wrote, instead of briefing a new worker from scratch.
From there, we vary five things:
- Where the lead uses workers. We instruct the lead agent with two main prompts, which differ in how much guidance they give. The minimal prompt tells the lead that it is in charge of a team and asks it to give workers distinct, independent tasks, but leaves everything else, from how many workers to use to how to decompose the task, to the lead. The PIV prompt adds a structured workflow of exploring and planning (P), implementing (I), and verifying (V), and asks the lead to use workers in all three stages.
- How the lead waits. A blocking lead waits for its workers to report back and does nothing in the meantime. An asynchronous lead keeps working while they run, and has two more tools,
wait_for_updates
to wait for the next report andlist_agents
to check on its workers. - Which models play which role. Does every agent on the team need the strongest, most expensive model? We test this with two kinds of teams. In a homogeneous team, the lead and its workers all run the same model. In a heterogeneous team, the lead keeps the strong model, but the workers run a cheaper one. Think of a senior engineer who directs the work and makes critical decisions, with junior engineers doing most of the legwork.
- How many workers there are. Is a bigger team always better? To explore this, we compare two setups. In the first, the lead decides on its own how many workers it needs. In the second, we fix the team size at two, four, eight, or sixteen workers and see how reward and cost change as the team grows.
- How agents communicate. By default, all communication goes through the lead, which hands out each subtask and receives each worker's report. In one set of runs, we provide agents with a
send_message
tool and let them message each other directly.
Figure 2. Two leads hand out the same subtasks, and each worker run takes the same time. The blocking lead sits idle until its workers report back. The asynchronous lead keeps working and starts the second round as soon as the first reports arrive. Bars are spans of work, downward arrows are calls to delegate_agent
, and upward arrows carry reports back to the lead. Timings are illustrative.
ProgramBench
We test these choices on ProgramBench [[6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03546)], a benchmark of 200 programs to rebuild from scratch. In each task, the agent starts from an empty workspace with the original program's executable, which it can run but not read, and that program's documentation. It has to probe the program to discover its interface, edge cases, and behavior, then write a new implementation that behaves the same way. We score each task by the share of a hidden suite of behavioral tests that the rebuilt program passes, and average this score over tasks to get the reward we report throughout.2
The tasks range from small command-line utilities like jq and ripgrep to large systems like SQLite, FFmpeg, and the PHP interpreter. The most challenging remain far out of reach. On FFmpeg, the best entry on the [public leaderboard](https://programbench.com) passes about 10% of tests.
Each task needs all three stages of the workflow, figuring out what the program does, writing it, and checking it against the original. That makes ProgramBench a good testbed for seeing which stages benefit from extra agents.
Figure 3. One ProgramBench task, dsq
, a command-line tool that runs SQL queries over JSON, CSV, and other data files. The top panel is a solo Sol agent with the minimal prompt, and the bottom panel an asynchronous Sol team with the PIV prompt. The solo agent writes its program as one Python file, while the team splits it into modules, some written by workers. The team panel follows the files of one run, commands are simplified from the agents' own, and timings are illustrative.
We focus primarily on three GPT-5.6 models, Luna, Terra, and Sol, in increasing order of capability and cost. Unless noted otherwise, we ran each configuration three times on all 200 ProgramBench tasks and report averages over the three runs for reward, total cost, and total wall-clock time. A single task's score varied from run to run with a standard deviation of about 6 points, but the benchmark-wide average was far steadier, with a standard deviation of 0.5 points for a typical configuration and 1.4 for the noisiest. Every configuration ran on the same tasks, so we compare each team with its solo baseline task by task and report 95% confidence intervals of those differences.
We also ran Commit0-Lite [[7](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01769)], a set of 16 Python libraries whose implementations have been removed. The agent is given each library's repository skeleton, documentation, and unit tests, and has to fill in the code so that the tests pass. In ProgramBench, the agent has to work out what to build by running the original program. In Commit0, these provided materials spell it out, so the benchmark shows whether the same stages pay off when the specification is already given. With only 16 tasks, we use it as a secondary check.
Teams outperform solo agents, at a cost
We start with the simplest comparison, a single Sol agent against a team of Sol agents. With the same minimal prompt, a blocking team passed 61.8% of tests on average, against 52.1% for the solo agent. Giving the solo agent the PIV prompt closed part of that gap (57.7%), but a blocking team with the PIV prompt still came out about 5 points ahead (63.1%).
We also ran both prompts with an asynchronous lead, which can keep working while its workers run. All four Sol teams cost between 4 and 7 times as much as the corresponding solo agent. With the PIV prompt, the asynchronous team finished in 19.5% less time than the blocking one and reached about the same reward.
With the minimal prompt, the asynchronous team finished in 60% less time, but its lead did more of the work itself, delegating just 4.4 times per task, compared to 6.1 for the blocking lead. Its team gained only 3.8 points over the minimally prompted solo agent, against 9.7 for the blocking team, and at 55.9% it even fell below the PIV-prompted solo agent (57.7%).
Workers pay off most in planning
To find out where workers pay off, we instructed the lead to delegate subtasks to workers in just a single stage, while doing the other two stages itself. Under exploration and planning (P), workers run the program to learn its behavior and draft a plan, and the lead implements and verifies. Under implementation (I), workers write the code. Under verification (V), workers test the lead's implementation.
Planning was the clear winner. Among asynchronous teams, a lead that delegates only planning matched the reward of one that delegates every stage (63.6% against 63.2%) at half the cost ($249 against $510). Measured as reward gained per $100 of added cost, planning was about twice as efficient as the next-best stage.3
For example, on dsq
, the solo agent with the PIV prompt passed 60% of its tests on average. Teams that delegate only planning passed 79% with an asynchronous lead and 76% with a blocking one, and each of their six runs beat every solo run. Teams that delegate implementation or verification passed only 58% to 71%.
The reason lies in the benchmark's design. The target program is a black box, so its behavior has to be discovered by running it. Planning workers do this in parallel, each probing a different part of the program's interface and handing the lead what it found. The lead then writes the code itself, with a much fuller picture of what to build.
Other works have reported related findings. Factory's validator begins by probing the reference program to build an executable standard of what "done" means, before any code is written [[4](https://factory.com/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks)]. Carlini's C-compiler team got unstuck on the Linux kernel by using GCC as an oracle to compare against [[1](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler)]. In each case, knowing exactly what to build was the bottleneck, and putting compute there paid off.
Commit0 shows the other side of this. There, the repository already lays out what to build, and implementation, not planning, was the most effective stage to delegate in eight of our ten team setups. However, frontier models like GPT-5.6 Sol are close to saturating Commit0, with a capable solo agent already passing every test on 12 of the 16 tasks, which leaves only four tasks where the team could do better, so we treat this as suggestive rather than conclusive.
Planning workers can be cheap
If planning workers mostly gather info

# The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

[Interact with the data(opens in a new window)](https://agenticeu.openai.chatgpt.site/) [Download the PDF(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/europes-agentic-opportunity.pdf)

Loading…

Share

Across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT. 

We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents [a substantial share of activity⁠](https://openai.com/signals/enterprise-data/). In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

*This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated users.*

The agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

But we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

*Frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.*

The takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies [globally⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/entrepreneurship/total-number-of-firms).

These figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

> “Europe is now in a new era of AI, with tools that can carry out tasks for people. More than half of the AI use among our EU enterprise and business customers now involves these tools, and the number of small business users has grown 8x across the region. Yet there is still plenty of room for AI use to grow across the EU. Giving people the tools, skills and confidence to use AI well will help build stronger businesses and growing economies, with benefits felt across Europe.”

Sarah Friar, Chief Financial Officer, OpenAI

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
body:
13th October 2026 - Link Blog
[Redesigning source control at Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) ([via](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50073633)) Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.
They included a chart showing those changes. I [had Claude modify their chart](https://claude.ai/share/aefcdd4a-9364-40c1-927a-29bf445894fc) ([code here](https://gist.github.com/simonw/4a16dff066fd9763faf8642f797905be)) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:
This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.
"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:
The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.
When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G [replied](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50073633#50079495):
Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.
As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:
Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

title: llm-gemini 0.35
body:
13th October 2026
I added support to [llm-gemini](https://github.com/simonw/llm-gemini) for the [new Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/) model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.
Here are [the low, medium and high pelicans](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2Fd741e4420dea14c460f0108ac22dbc26). As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their [staff have invested in SVG specifically](https://twitter.com/sunjiao123sun_/status/2024555516551372920) (and who have [boasted about their pelicans](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Feb/19/gemini-31-pro/#jeff-dean) before.)
Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:
The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.
Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.
One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish [the total cost to run their benchmark](https://artificialanalysis.ai/#total-cost-tabs) using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.
When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.
(I [used ChatGPT to edit that chart](https://chatgpt.com/share/6acebe13-5378-83e8-bf2f-9f4d05b206f4)! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)
Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's [Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F9589ff9e0c977bbf3b012b7a11f5bd71), here's [a Fabergé egg](https://tools.simonwillison.net/blender-viewer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fstatic.simonwillison.net%2Fstatic%2Fcors-allow%2F2026%2Fgemini-4-astra-egg.blend) it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared [a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles](https://twitter.com/fofrai/status/2110043023954284889). title: Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely
body:
Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely
Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/), while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google.
This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, [Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/scan-for-good) used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process.
Today, we are beginning to roll out [Argon broadly](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), as well as expanding our Fairwind Program to additional trusted cyber defenders. To do this well, we grappled with two big questions:
- How do we build the right safety guardrails? If Argon can help defenders find complex software bugs or help scientists design experiments, how do we stop bad actors from using it to launch cyberattacks or create biological threats? (Misuse)
- Can we trust the model to do the job the right way? As models become more resourceful problem-solvers, how do we make sure they don’t cut corners, cross boundaries, or make incorrect high-stakes decisions? (Misalignment and Prompt Injection)
Our [full Safety and Security Report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf) systematically covers our set of defenses. Below are some highlights from how we approached these two questions for Gemini 4 Argon.
Misuse prevention across high-risk domains
The same coding and reasoning improvements that enabled Argon to find and patch vulnerabilities also drove better performance on our cybersecurity tests — solving all 12 of the end-to-end simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in our previous generation. In biology evaluations, unguarded versions of the model also showed a much stronger ability to help troubleshoot complex lab procedures step by step. Following our [Frontier Safety Framework](https://deepmind.google/blog/strengthening-our-frontier-safety-framework/), since we saw elevated capabilities in the cyber and biological domains, we put our next-generation set of frontier safeguards in place across both areas.
First, when it comes to potentially dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials, Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly twofold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models. Second, we wrap the model in three layers of real-time protection; this is to prevent determined attackers that might try to jailbreak (i.e. trick) the model by disguising a dangerous request as a harmless story or breaking it into dozens of small questions over several weeks. Here is how these protections work:
- Input screening: Smaller models check incoming requests and conversation context for malicious intent or dangerous requests.
- Internal introspection: Even if a request is cleverly disguised to look harmless, small transformers ("activation probes") read the model’s internal neural signals and are trained to spot when it is activating knowledge about cyberattacks or biological threats.
- Continuous monitoring: As the model reasons and writes its response across multiple steps, we combine these signals and take action when necessary such as cutting off the agent mid-stream if the responses become problematic.
Combining real-time protection, faster fixes for new jailbreaks and enhanced monitoring for recurring misuse has made our systems better at preventing real-world harm. For instance, external bio jailbreak red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for.
Real-time misalignment monitoring
Misalignment can sometimes mean an agent deciding on its own to pursue a goal different to what was intended by the user. Because Argon is much better than earlier models at understanding the environment it is running in, we test carefully for that kind of behavior. For example, we ran realistic "honeypot" tests to see if the model would increase its ability to take covert actions, such as sabotaging safety monitoring. We didn't find any instances of that behavior.
But what we do see in practice today is something much more familiar: an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given. When a resourceful assistant is told to get a task done and runs into a locked door, it can treat that obstacle as just another puzzle to solve.
This is why we trained Gemini 4 Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause to ask for human confirmation. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, attempts to take a shortcut or cheat on the task dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance for recent Gemini models.
And while this is a major step forward, when a model runs millions of complex tasks, even a rare misstep will eventually show up. As a second line of defense, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads both the agent’s actions and its internal "scratchpad" (its step-by-step chain of thought) in real time, blocking severe boundary violations before they happen and flagging serious internal cases for human responders. (We continually harden our training and evaluation environments against potential escapes. You can read more about this in our [agent control roadmap](https://deepmind.google/blog/securing-the-future-of-ai-agents/)). We run this monitor in our products, on our internal coding agents, during our training runs, and during our capability evaluations.
When training tasks were difficult or when training environments were flawed, our monitor caught the model, in rare instances, creatively attempting to game the test. The model attempted to escalate container privileges to alter grading scripts, read answers from the test runner's memory, and in one case it even crashed the evaluation sandbox to avoid getting scored for a failed run. While we use these catches to fix flawed tasks, we do not use them to otherwise intervene with the training process to avoid overfitting to the monitor.
And we always follow one rule: we don’t penalize the model for what it writes in its chain of thought during training. Here’s an example to illustrate why: in a reinforcement learning training run where a shortcut penalty was accidentally applied to the chain of thought, openly discussed shortcuts dropped by 61%, but that did not mean the model took less shortcuts. Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%). Avoiding thought penalties encourages the model’s reasoning to stay transparent and monitorable.
Prompt injection resistance
To trust an agent to do the job right, we need to ensure that malicious content the agent comes across cannot trick it to take a harmful action. When agents browse webpages or read code, they can encounter hidden, malicious instructions, or context designed to hijack their task. Through built-in adversarial training and real-time security checks, Argon leads in prompt injection robustness on Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%.
The above safety and security defenses represent only three categories of our extensive defense-in-depth stack. To learn more about our approach to safety testing and mitigations, read our full [Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf) and see the [Gemini 4 Argon Model Card](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/Model-Cards/Gemini-4-Argon-Model-Card.pdf).

title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
body:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.
