title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
body:
Text Generation • 24B • Updated • 2.88k • 354
[
](#run-fast-private-agents-on-device-with-lfm25-24b-a2b)
Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
[Team Article](/blog)
[LFM2.5-24B-A2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B)is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.
- Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19.
- Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap.
- Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.
[
](#how-we-built-a-reasoning-agent-with-2b-active-parameters)
How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters
LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on [LFM2-24B-A2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2-24B-A2B) and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an [in-place tokenizer expansion](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/tokenizer-expansion) doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.
Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:
- Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
- Teacher specialization
- Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.
- MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.
- Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as
[OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai),[Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com),[Pi](https://pi.dev), and[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai).
[
](#benchmark-results)
Benchmark results
We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.
| Benchmark | LFM2.5-24B-A2B | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it | Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AutomationBench | 27.69 | 8.72 | 5.46 | 2.61 |
| BFCLv4 | 65.01 | 65.00 | 57.09 | 53.78 |
| ToolSandbox | 80.71 | 75.02 | 72.09 | 75.13 |
| LiveClaw | 48.09 | 38.19 | 41.25 | 37.72 |
| PinchBench | 83.18 | 89.93 | 77.12 | 84.20 |
| τ³-Bench Banking | 8.04 | 7.63 | 4.54 | 7.01 |
| WebArena Verified | 26.75 | 37.62 | 25.62 | 28.69 |
| GPQA Diamond | 74.42 | 83.69 | 74.90 | 72.42 |
| AA-Omniscience | -24.90 | -24.35 | -59.39 | -3.58 |
| HLE | 7.40 | 7.69 | 8.57 | 5.65 |
| IFEval | 96.75 | 93.06 | 92.00 | 94.19 |
| IFBench | 74.69 | 64.21 | 47.44 | 71.67 |
| Multi-IF | 84.38 | 81.53 | 82.19 | 82.34 |
| MATH-500 | 96.04 | 96.73 | 95.66 | 96.40 |
| SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) | 51.00 | 66.20 | 25.80 | 53.40 |
| SciCode | 32.71 | 37.35 | 35.42 | 27.78 |
*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.
For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.
These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.
[
](#inference-speed-on-cpu-and-gpu)
Inference speed on CPU and GPU
LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.
Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.
GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.
[
](#how-to-use-lfm25-24b-a2b)
How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B
Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.
Install the latest version of transformers
(compatible with transformers>=5.0.0
):
pip install -U transformers
Then load and run the model:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer
model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id,
device_map="auto",
dtype="bfloat16",
# attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)
prompt = "What is C. elegans?"
input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
add_generation_prompt=True,
return_tensors="pt",
tokenize=True,
)["input_ids"].to(model.device)
output = model.generate(
input_ids,
do_sample=True,
temperature=0.1,
top_k=50,
repetition_penalty=1.05,
max_new_tokens=512,
streamer=streamer,
)
[
](#use-it-in-your-agent-harness)
Use it in your agent harness
Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:
hermes config set model.provider custom
hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1
hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B
hermes config set model.context_length 131072
hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions
hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true
The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080
, vLLM uses 8000
, SGLang uses 30000
, and LM Studio uses 1234
. See the [model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B) for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and [our guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses) for the full setup. Check out our [release blog](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b) for video examples.
[
](#get-started-with-lfm25-24b-a2b)
Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:
- Download:
[LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base)and[LFM2.5-24B-A2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B)on Hugging Face. - Use in your harness: follow our
[guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses)on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. - Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our
[fine-tuning tutorials](https://github.com/Liquid4All/cookbook/tree/main/finetuning/notebooks).
We can't wait to see what you build.

Citation

title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
body:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.

title: Copilot to autopilot: Why no single safeguard is enough
body:
Published Time: 2026-10-13T16:03:25+00:00

Markdown Content:
It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments.

We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix.

And that is where the demo stops being a demo.

Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk.

> Safe autonomy requires a stack.

This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack.

## What do we even mean by “agent”?

Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here.

An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch.

Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it.

> Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it.

Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it.

Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits.

## Authorization over intelligence

The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls.

Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take?

A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone.

> The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence.

**The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence.** Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game.

## The mental model: Four boundaries, layered

Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point.

![Image 1: The concentric “defense in depth” diagram, with an untrusted LLM at the core wrapped by four boundaries (Identity, Tool, Mutation, Time).](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Designer-5-1024x683.png)

The concentric “defense in depth” diagram, with an untrusted LLM at the core wrapped by four boundaries (Identity, Tool, Mutation, Time).

Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go.

### Layer 1: The agent never has more access than you

The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access.

### Layer 2: One tool interface, not a bare shell

The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the _unbounded_ one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or a clean audit trail around bash. But a command line invoked as one narrow, declared tool, behind the interface, is fine.

> The framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy.

This is why the framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy. You want both, chosen by trust level. Put everything behind the tool interface, then pick the implementation per call: a plain function or a sandboxed CLI for low-risk local work inside the trust boundary, and MCP for anything that crosses it, because MCP gives you least privilege, credential isolation, structured audit, human approval hooks, and rate limiting for free. You can secure a CLI, too, but only by paying for per-user sandboxes with tightly limited access, and even then, you can’t match per-tool granularity.

### Layer 3: Read freely, pause before you write

Diagnostics run on their own. Anything that mutates production stops and waits for a human. This sounds obvious and is surprisingly hard to enforce, because the temptation is to let “safe-looking” writes through. We do not. The gate is code in the execution engine, not a line in a prompt, and trust to skip it is earned per procedure and per action type—never granted to a model because the model is smart.

### Layer 4: The agent that learns to stop being an agent

The first time we see an incident, the agent reasons through it end to end, which is expensive and non-deterministic. But most incidents aren’t novel. When the same reasoning path succeeds enough times, we crystallize it into a deterministic playbook that runs with zero model calls. The agent becomes a discovery mechanism for new problems, not a permanent tax on old ones. Less live reasoning means lower cost, higher reproducibility, and a smaller surface for both hallucination and attack, all at once.

![Image 2: Unconstrained agent vs. traditional automation vs. the composed stack, across Safety, Auditability, Compliance-fit, Reproducibility, Flexibility, Novel-incident handling, Speed, and Cost efficiency. No approach wins everywhere; the composed stack is the only shape that stays large where operations need it.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Designer-4-1024x683.png)

Unconstrained agent vs. traditional automation vs. the composed stack, across Safety, Auditability, Compliance-fit, Reproducibility, Flexibility, Novel-incident handling, Speed, and Cost efficiency. No approach wins everywhere; the composed stack is the only shape that stays large where operations need it.

## Why one layer is never enough

Let me make this concrete with the incident from the top, because it shows where a single control would have failed.

The agent gets show interface status back from a device. That output is unstructured text, and this is the kind of work a language model is good at, so we let it parse. But we don’t let it decide. The output of the model is constrained to a schema, validated, and only then handed to ordinary deterministic code that chooses the action:

```
# errdisabled- recovery.yaml  (excerpt) 
steps: 
  - id: parse-status 
    type: ai-extract          # LLM parses unstructured CLI output into typed JSON 
    prompt: "Extract interface, status, vlan from the CLI output." 
    schema: 
      interface: string 
      status: enum[connected, errdisabled, notconnect] 
      vlan: int 
 
  - id: validate 
    type: assert              # deterministic: reject anything off-schema 
    rule: "status in [connected, errdisabled, notconnect]" 
 
  - id: decide 
    type: condition           # deterministic: no model in the decision 
    when: "status == 'errdisabled'" 
    then: recover-interface   # a WRITE step -> pauses for human approval 
    else: no-action
```

This is the pattern we call deterministic skeleton, probabilistic filling. The language model is the semantic parser. It is never the decision-maker, and it never holds the credential that executes the change.

> Deterministic skeleton, probabilistic filling.

Now watch what happens on a harder request. Ask the same system to generate a BGP configuration for a new device, and it will produce something that looks completely correct. It will also, often enough to matter, invent an ASN, reference a route policy that doesn’t exist, or quietly miss a datacenter-specific convention that no amount of prompting reliably teaches. Config generation is novel synthesis, which is the least reliable thing a model does, and it’s also the most risky, because the output goes near production.

So, walk the counterfactual, one layer at a time.

*   Remove **identity** and the agent runs with “god-mode” credentials. The hallucinated config gets pushed with authority no human on that call actually had.
*   Remove the **tool** interface and give it a bare shell, and there is no way to even name “pushing a BGP config” as a distinct, authorizable, auditable action. It’s just another command, with nowhere to attach RBAC or an approval gate.
*   Remove the **mutation** gate and the invented ASN reaches the device, because the config looked fine and nothing stopped to ask.
*   Remove **time** / crystallization and you pay full, non-deterministic reasoning cost on every routine incident forever, which means you’re running the riskiest execution mode eve

title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
body:
OCT. 13, 2026
Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.
You can see this leap in capability on the [Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark](https://github.com/embodiedreasoning/ERQA), which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.
As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:
- Robot control → Mobile manipulation with
[MuJoCo](https://mujoco.org/)practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models. - Real2Sim → Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches.
- Physical understanding → Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation.
- Research and self-improvement → Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware.
Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin.
Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside.
Prompt:
There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left.
Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin.
Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing.
Plain text
Copied
Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns.
Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle.
Prompt:
[Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json]
Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug.
## Execution Discipline
- Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`.
## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png)
- `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base
- `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right
- `+Z`: Height above table | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`)
- `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center
- `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line
- `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y)
- `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis
## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow
1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`:
`curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`).
2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1:
- Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done`
- Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done`
- Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done`

title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
body:
Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
[Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/) is now globally available today for developers and enterprises via the API in [AI Studio](https://ai.google.dev/aistudio) and [Gemini platform](https://console.cloud.google.com/agent-platform/studio/multimodal;mode=prompt?model=gemini-4-argon®ion=global), for [Google AI Ultra subscribers](https://one.google.com/about/google-ai-plans/) in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/), and Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the [Gemini app](http://gemini.google/) and [AI Mode in Search](http://aimode.google/).
Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its depth and precision across multi-step tasks leads Argon to outperform other frontier models on [benchmarks across domains](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/#workingharder), ranking #1 on the [Vals Index](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index), which measures model performance across critical economic sectors like finance, coding, legal, and tax work.
The model launches today at an [introductory price](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing)
[1](#footnote-1)
of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens (with cached input tokens at 95% off).
Teams at Google, across enterprises, and in the research community have already been using Argon to land significant impact across fields:
- To solve major engineering problems like large codebase refactoring and optimizations
- To optimize business workflows across domains like legal, finance, and science
- To find and patch critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities
- To enable novel breakthroughs in quantum computing, nuclear fusion, and life sciences
Solving complex engineering tasks
At Google, we’ve been using Argon on our hardest engineering problems. Over the past few weeks, software engineers have been shipping high-quality code faster than ever. Argon in Antigravity has helped teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third.
- Untangling browser feature code in Chrome: Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase.
[Piping multiple clean code changes at a time](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/540709814), Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.
- Optimizing a production Python codebase in hours: Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source
[Agent Development Kit](https://github.com/google/adk-python)(ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their[.agents/skills](https://github.com/google/adk-python/tree/main/.agents/skills)rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations,[now live in google/adk-python](https://github.com/google/adk-python/commit/1754b3eeb6cdb2c16e3b30619a12066623df132e), that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%. Read the[engineering deep dive](https://developers.googleblog.com/optimizing-a-200000-line-python-codebase-overnight-with-gemini-4-argon)to learn more. - Quantum chemistry open-source package optimization: xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official
[xTB repository on GitHub](https://github.com/grimme-lab/xtb/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Ag8j39+%28created%3A%3E2026-10-05+created%3A%3C2026-10-10%29). - Making our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast: Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the
[upstream pull requests](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Alucianommartins+%28created%3A%3E2026-10-05+created%3A%3C2026-10-10%29)(optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes. - Delivering complex 3D visualizations: Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models. Using slash commands like /goal and prompting for multi-agent loops with custom skills in Antigravity, Googlers are using Argon to prototype complex 3D visualizations, high-fidelity games, and interactive animations in vanilla code that can be rendered directly in the browser.
Transforming critical business and professional workflows
Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to help with high-stakes professional workflows. It communicates clearly, keeping you in the loop, and follows style instructions better than any of our previous Gemini models. Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.
Enterprise customers and startups in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.
Using its advanced reasoning and multimodal capabilities while maintaining strict grounding, Argon excels in deep multimodal document comprehension, longitudinal data analysis, and interactive analytical sandboxes.
Accelerating real-world impact with researchers and domain experts
Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are already using Argon to push the boundaries of cyber defense, science, math, and robotics. It’s helping cyber defenders and researchers test hypotheses, autonomously audit critical codebases and formal proofs, and catch subtle zero-day vulnerabilities and logic flaws.
Bringing state-of-the-art cyber capabilities to more trusted defenders
Starting today, we’re beginning expansion to hundreds of additional [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/) partners.
[Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/) is already using Argon for its "[Scan for Good](https://www.wiz.io/blog/scan-for-good-critical-ai-exposures)" initiative, which protects critical infrastructure for the public good and for free. With early access to the model, Wiz has demonstrated Argon's real-world impact across multiple high-stakes sectors:
- Securing sensitive government data: As part of a long-standing cyber resilience program and in collaboration with a federal agency, Argon helped to proactively identify and remediate a gap that risked exposing sensitive data and government infrastructure. This effort helped prevent against the exposure of critical security sector development details and unauthorized access to specialized models.
- Protecting critical healthcare infrastructure: Wiz also used Argon to protect vital healthcare infrastructure. By chaining complex vulnerabilities, the model helped the team discover and quickly fix a public file download bypass that exposed a master key and granted administrator access. Argon went beyond spotting a vulnerability to proactively safeguarding hundreds of thousands of private patient records.
Unlocking new scientific breakthroughs
Argon is already having real-world impact across the scientific community — enabling novel discovery for scientists and experts across multiple domains.
- Quantum computing: Argon is helping our researchers accelerate progress across both quantum error correction and algorithm design. To help error decoders keep pace with quantum hardware in real-time, Argon translated an internal version of
[AlphaQubit](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/alphaqubit-quantum-error-correction/), our ML quantum error correction decoder, into a single, highly optimized hardware kernel — nearly doubling its inference throughput so we can deploy larger, more capable models and scale to larger quantum devices, while continuing to meet strict real-time thresholds. Argon is also reducing spacetime costs for quantum subroutines. For arcsin, a building block in recent quantum simulation algorithms, an implementation written by Argon and formally verified in Lean cuts spacetime cost by more than 100x compared to a published quantum CORDIC baseline, a step toward a standard library of optimized quantum circuits. - Nuclear fusion: Stellarators are incredibly complex machines that represent a leading candidate for limitless clean fusion energy, but optimizing their 3D magnetic fields is famously difficult. Since 1967, a long-standing hypothesis known as “Grad’s conjecture” assumed that finding exact mathematical solutions for these fields was impossible, until recent counterexamples were found, including by Professor Matt Landreman (University of Maryland). Now, a team at Google alongside Professor Landreman has discovered a
[broader class of counterexamples to Grad's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07304). These new solutions give the fusion community reliable benchmarks to test their stellarator simulations codes, which are valuable tools for future designs. - Rare disease research: Researchers at Gamow Labs used Argon to analyze de-identified genomes from newborns with rare developmental lung disorders. In one case, Argon pinpointed a chromosomal rearrangement that routine software missed for years, and explained why it went undetected. On private Gamow Labs evals derived from real clinical and lab data, Argon topped on
[RareBench](https://gamowlabs.com/benchmarks)(57% on assistance with rare-disease diagnosis) and[LabBench](https://gamowlabs.com/benchmarks)(52.2% on wet-lab reasoning). These advances point to faster diagnosis for families facing rare conditions. See[blog](https://gamowlabs.com/bringing-expert-genome-interpretation-to-every-nicu)[2](#footnote-2)for more details. - Enzyme design: Engineering enzymes with precise reactivity is notoriously slow, often demanding months of bespoke model tuning and candidate screening. Serine esterases are a class of enzymes that cut ester bonds on targeted molecules, widely used in recycling, and the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, biofuels and detergents. Our scientists worked with Argon to design serine esterases, targeting the benchmark molecule 4MU-acetate that glows under UV light once its ester bonds are broken. In a matter of hours, Argon assembled relevant data, performed model tuning and identified multiple biochemistry-inspired filters to get to a final set of five novel designs. Subsequent laboratory testing confirmed robust catalytic activity across these designs. The speed and ease of successful enzyme generation demonstrates the potential for rapid acceleration in enzyme engineering in fields such as biomanufacturing, green chemistry, and drug development.
To further advance the pace of research, we’re offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are [now open](https://forms.gle/WvmBbPvRbpKG

title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
body:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.


Speaker info:
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/michelegrantleadership/

Timestamps:
00:00 - From a working agent to organizational trust
2:34 - An illustrative acquisition integration scenario
4:47 - Measure value against a baseline
6:29 - Accountability across three lines of ownership
8:14 - The Human Works Standard
9:54 - Decision logs and the agent inventory
11:51 - Four stages of autonomy
12:50 - Independent sampling and missed issues
13:29 - What the framework lets leaders decide

See[blog](https://gamowlabs.com/bringing-expert-genome-interpretation-to-every-nicu)[2](#footnote-2)for more details. - Enzyme design: Engineering enzymes with precise reactivity is notoriously slow, often demanding months of bespoke model tuning and candidate screening. Serine esterases are a class of enzymes that cut ester bonds on targeted molecules, widely used in recycling, and the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, biofuels and detergents. Our scientists worked with Argon to design serine esterases, targeting the benchmark molecule 4MU-acetate that glows under UV light once its ester bonds are broken. In a matter of hours, Argon assembled relevant data, performed model tuning and identified multiple biochemistry-inspired filters to get to a final set of five novel designs. Subsequent laboratory testing confirmed robust catalytic activity across these designs. The speed and ease of successful enzyme generation demonstrates the potential for rapid acceleration in enzyme engineering in fields such as biomanufacturing, green chemistry, and drug development.

title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
body:
A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate.

When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval.

title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
body:
Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation.

Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations, compare visits and make spatial evidence available to the people and systems that need it.

body:
Hi folks,
quick aside: I’m working on something for non-developers who don’t quite know what to use personal agents for. Maybe you chat with it but you’re not quite seeing why everyone’s raving about them. If that’s you, please reply to this email. I’m looking for ~20 people to test a new thing. I’ll invite you to a slack channel.
Ok so X is arguing whether software is dead…again. These takes are like assholes, everyone’s got one. Including me.
Software isn’t dead. More code is being written than ever before (probably). Something may be dead, but we just don’t quite what it is.
I use far fewer SaaS tools than I ever have before - I actually got my personal agent (grok bot btw) to go through our business subscriptions and saved $6k/year - got rid of webflow, resend, cal, zoom and a bunch more. If I do want to use any tools, I now think of whether my bots can use it. I never have to look at the interface, it’s all done by software talking to software - aka ‘headless’.
And I’m making sites for all sorts of things. I spun up a site to review all my subscriptions so I could easily go through them and mark which to keep or kill. Then I just throw away the site after I use it. (or more accurately, it just sits somewhere untouched forever).
The biggest problem I see is that most people don’t see themselves as ‘builders’. They don’t think to build a site for tasks (todos, email triage, recipes, kids calendars, etc). But that’s my default. I hate reading words, ironically. Give me something visual any day.
I think agents will be the form factor that gets everyday people to make software, as long as it doesn’t feel like it. The problem right now is those agents are proactive (sometimes) that give you work to do (aren’t you working for me!?) and they don’t hand you software unless you ask for it.
If you were given a site with your todos, I’d bet you’d want to customise the colours or layout or something. When we had MySpace pages we customised them with music, themes, layouts. Some people went further and learnt HTML & CSS to customise further.
Software ‘you’ create should just feel like customising something that’s already yours.
Other related things I’ve been thinking about:
slop is a slur, as is vibe coding. Developers love to shit on us for our agents writing slop code. But if it works, is secure and performant, why does it really matter? It matters more if you’re providing critical infra for customers paying you money, sure. But for your own tools and sites, slop works. I also believe it’s an agents job to deal with slop, my code is bad? cool - go fix it then.
slop → slope. You know how developers started? By writing awful code. We’re not trying to learn to write code, never mind good code. If we want to build stuff, of course there will be bumps in the road. For both groups, the way to get better is doing more of it and picking up the understanding of the system along the way.

Wonder Full is even stronger, just shy of Opus 5.5 everyday performance. It’s only available in the Muse Code subscriber plan for now (starts at $50/mo).

Sarah’s essay on the end of friction is a banger.
My personal agent of choice right now is Grok Bot. I still can’t test Muse in the UK (I’ve tried all the tricks). It’s fast, very capable and has a good interface. Dots needs to tighten up a bunch of stuff before I go back (and I had a call w/ OpenAI about my feedback 😬 ). I’m actually trying to do as much work as I can in Grok Bot to give it a fair shot and feel where there may be gaps. I spin up new bots for tasks, instead of considering them other teammates, then archive the bot when it’s done.
I went through 195 domains I have on 3 different platforms and cut my auto-renew bills down from $4k/year (!!!) to half that. And now it’s moving them all to one platform.
I’ve got one taking over my email triage (label + archive rules). But its a bit janky atm.
As with all of these tools, unfortunately for now, the best thing to do is just dive right into them and try and use them for as much as you can think of.
Grok Bot still has it’s annoyances - it can’t use my computer unless I remind it + happen to be on my computer, instead of my phone (think its a known issue).

title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
body:
A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings.

The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark.

title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
body:
[NVIDIA RTX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/) is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents.
Last week, [NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-rtx-spark-microsoft-windows-event/). Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark.
New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include:
- New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark:
- Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing.
- The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15.
[NVIDIA PAIR](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-on-rtx/personal-ai-router/)moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support.
- Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark:
- Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more.
- The
[NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/broadcasting/broadcast-app/)release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. - NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows.
- NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport.
- Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark:
- Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries.
- GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark.
- Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app.
- Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus:
- A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the
[NVIDIA App beta](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/nvidia-app/). - Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23.
- The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23.
- A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the
Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools
AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year.
From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents.
Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark
From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app.
These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC.
After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks.
Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions.
Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of [CUDA-X Skills](https://github.com/NVIDIA/skills).
NVIDIA is also releasing [AI playbooks](http://build.nvidia.com/rtx-spark) for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant.
Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark.
This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.
Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.
Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.
The Perfect PAIR
Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. [NVIDIA PAIR](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-on-rtx/personal-ai-router/), a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems.
The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements.
PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via [Github](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router) — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release.
Sparking Creativity
RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance.
Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark
Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows.
In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects.
The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds.
Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content
Available for download now, [NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/broadcasting/broadcast-app/) runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles.
A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app.
RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI
ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video.
RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow.
For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading.
Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction
Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download [Blender version 5.3](https://builder.blender.org/download/daily/) to get access.
Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time.
Code, Text and Deploy From RTX Spark
Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype.
RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud.
Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready
NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing:
- The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm.
- The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm,

title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
body:
A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs.

Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error.

[Higgsfield AI⁠(opens in a new window)](https://higgsfield.ai/) is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea. Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute. Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, users can create videos over 10 minutes long.

Longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work. According to Alex, with models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, it’s now possible for a single creator to execute high-end fashion campaigns from start to finish.

> “What’s most important for us at Higgsfield is to see that smaller creative teams can actually be more successful now with the power of models like GPT-6 Astra and GPT-Image-2.5.”

—Alex Mashrabov, CEO and co-founder, Higgsfield AI

## Making longer videos possible with GPT‑6 Astra

Higgsfield AI’s creative agents take on repetitive production tasks, such as creating multiple variations of a shot. With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling. Alex says that capability helps address one of creative AI’s hardest problems: maintaining consistency across longer videos.

The evidence can be seen on Higgsfield AI’s own YouTube channel, which Alex says has almost half a million subscribers. The channel teaches creatives how to use AI models and workflows. It used to require considerable manual effort for Higgsfield AI to produce that content. But with GPT‑6 Astra, the team has built a workflow that uses AI to generate instructional videos over 10 minutes long.

Being able to create longer instructional videos also matters to Alex personally. He supports rural schools in Kazakhstan and describes an early effort using GPT‑6 Astra’s visual understanding to identify topics students may be struggling with and create videos tailored to what they need to learn.

## More precise images for small businesses with GPT‑Image‑2.5

For small businesses creating promotional content, having readable text and precise infographics can be just as important as the image itself. GPT‑Image‑2.5 makes that kind of content possible for businesses without large production budgets, Alex says.

“GPT‑Image‑2.5 is state of the art and the first model of its kind that can reliably render the text and infographics on top of the imagery,” he says.

## Enabling a faster path from creative idea to product with Codex

Higgsfield AI builds its product through close collaboration between around 200 creatives and 100 engineers. Codex gives the creative team “the power of a really strong software engineer,” shares Alex.

Creatives use Codex to turn their ideas into software prototypes. Previously, bringing those prototypes into production required heavy involvement from front-end and back-end engineers. Now, Alex says GPT‑6 Astra reduces the work needed to bring those ideas into the product.

> “GPT-6 Astra can ship production-ready code, which was never possible before.”

—Alex Mashrabov, CEO and co-founder, Higgsfield AI

With less friction between prototyping and production, Alex says Higgsfield AI can develop and ship better products faster.

## Looking ahead to voice-to-video with GPT‑Live‑1

Next, Higgsfield AI wants creators to be able to describe an idea and see it take shape as they talk. Alex calls that vision “voice to movie,” with AI understanding a creator’s spoken intention and rendering their vision in real time.

He sees OpenAI’s advances in planning, tool calling, image generation, and voice bringing that experience closer. He describes its voice model as “best in class for voice understanding and just for regular communication.”

For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.
