title: Faster Fourier Transforms
body:
Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.
The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.
The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product.[1](#footnote-1) Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:
For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n2 arithmetic operations.
The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965.[2](#footnote-2) The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log2(n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.
To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.
Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log2(n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log2(n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?
Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is
I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.
Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.
Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead, I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.
First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that
That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time. All constants are equivalent.
Big-O notation is useful for shortcuts in algorithmic accounting, but it also allows for remarkable logical laziness. If we want a practically faster FFT, we want an algorithm that requires fewer than 50n operations for reasonably sized n. But O(n) does not mean 50 n. It could mean 1080 n. This would be considered a “linear time” algorithm. An algorithm that requires n + 1080 is also considered a linear time algorithm in the big-O regime. An algorithm that only has linear-time guarantees when n is greater than 1080 is also considered linear time. 1080 is approximately equal to the number of atoms in the known universe. That is why Richard Lipton and Ken Regan call algorithms with unfathomably large hidden constants [galactic algorithms](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-41422-0_20).
The OpenAI FFT algorithm is definitely galactic. The estimated values for C were 10100 when N=1012. So even when n=10100, the venerable Cooley-Tukey-Gauss FFT would be 1099 times faster.
So why is this new FFT result interesting? Well, note that in big-O notation, it is technically asymptotically faster than the Cooley-Tukey algorithm because
I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need
whatever the hell that number means.
Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.
“The model uses exact complex arithmetic.” That means it assumes you can store and multiply complex numbers at arbitrary precision. Indeed, the algorithm requires you to multiply complex numbers whose magnitudes grow superpolynomially with n. If you stored these numbers as bits, the memory requirement would effectively be exponential in the input length. It assumes you can multiply such arbitrarily large complex numbers together in a single operation. We do not have computers that can do this. So even if this theorem in main.pdf is “true” (no one knows, and I don’t care), it’s not actually solving the problem we set out to solve when looking for a faster FFT.
For people familiar with theoretical analyses of the FFT, that you need an absurd model of computation to break the FFT speed limit isn’t surprising. In 1973, [Jacques Morgenstern proved](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/321752.321761) that you couldn’t get a Fourier transform faster than ½ n log n if you required that complex coefficients used in the computation had bounded magnitude. That should have been the end of the story! But it wasn’t. People said Morgenstern’s restricted coefficient model was too restrictive. Forty years later, Nir Ailon showed that you couldn’t compute an FFT faster than n log n without severe [numerical](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.1307) [instabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.1741). This was also too restrictive for some people, I guess.
This new OpenAI result is thus less a mathematical breakthrough and more an oddity of computer scientists being bad at formalizing their design specifications. The “theoretical” definition of a computer is very far removed from the computers we actually build. The “faster” Fourier transform is merely an example where theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle. The solution is like what happens when you set computational bot streams at impossible problems and find them [engaging in illegal hacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI_rogue_agent_breach_of_Hugging_Face).
Many of the other “big” results in this OpenAI slopository could be critiqued in the same way. For example, one of those results was a galactic algorithm to multiply two matrices in O(n^2.25) operations. The construction used in the paper does not let you even estimate the constant that hides inside big O.[3](#footnote-3) It may as well be infinite, computable only with the divine music of the spheres.
Still, if written substantially better, these papers would have made it into the most prestigious publication venues for the theory of computer science (i.e., refereed conference proceedings from STOC or FOCS).[4](#footnote-4) The matrix multiplication paper would have likely won awards. But neither of these has anything to do with computers!
This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”
AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.
[1](#footnote-anchor-1)
Kids these days call it cosine similarity.
[2](#footnote-anchor-2)
The wikipedia page says it should be credited to Gauss in 1805! Proper credit assignment is a perennial problem in academia.
[3](#footnote-anchor-3)
That one shows that for every epsilon greater than 0, there is a constant C so that T(n) <= n^(2.25 +epsilon + C/log(n)). No matter which queries I try, I can’t get an OpenAI model to give a quantitative estimate of C. Whatever!
[4](#footnote-anchor-4)
Another bad tradition is computer science choosing its most prestigious venues as hastily reviewed conference proceedings.
One nice thing about proving that something is possible epsilon faster than O(f(n)) time is that you can stop looking for a proof that the best you can do is O(f(n)).
Thanks for writing this up. A few weeks ago Anthropic publushed a blog post about "using claude to speed up protein structure prediction." I did a little testing myself and found that basically 100% of the "speedup" was from turning on cuda graphs and all the "optimized kernels" did not add much. Good (in some cosmic sense) to see that the pattern is similar for these math results.

title: From Earth to Orbit, France’s Ecosystem Delivers Agentic Computing at Scale With NVIDIA
body:
Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application.
France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork.
The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack.
Sovereign AI Infrastructure
France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology.
[Bull](https://www.bull.com/en/product-news/nvidia-vera-rubin-ultra) is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2.
Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by [Loft Orbital](http://loftorbital.com/orbitworks-launches-first-spacecraft-of-the-largest-ai-powered-satellite-constellation-with-nvidia-edge-ai-onboard) and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks, a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space, the satellite is flying [NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin](https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.nvidia.com%2Fen-us%2Fautonomous-machines%2Fembedded-systems%2F&data=05%7C02%7Clmekrez%40nvidia.com%7C4d0da41d383b4700c32808df256e61a5%7C43083d15727340c1b7db39efd9ccc17a%7C0%7C0%7C639270828236369551%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=c9qOnB3r3tMshO3VBqYOpRl6%2FcPmwB6BKaId27tbaW0%3D&reserved=0) edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit.
Open Models
[NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data.
LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement, making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations.
In financial services, [SBS](https://sbs-software.com/news/sbs-launches-bankings-first-sovereign-ai-platform/) is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA.
Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries.
[Fondation Inria](https://www.fondation-inria.fr/accelerating-open-source-ai-adoption/), with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year.
Agents at Work Across Industries
Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France.
L’Oréal is integrating [NVIDIA ALCHEMI](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-x-libraries/alchemi) into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients.
[Mirakl ](https://www.mirakl.com/blogs/agentic-commerce/why-mirakl-builds-on-open-source-ai-and-what-it-delivers-for-ecommerce-businesses/)has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours.
[Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/vestiaire-collective-liquidity-photoroom) are demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance.
[Omi](https://www.omi.so/resources/blog/omi-productdrop-brings-product-accuracy-to-genai-with-nvidia) helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference.
In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA [Cosmos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/cosmos/) open world models, Nemotron and [Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses.
Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos.
Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care.
In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment
In quantum, [Alice & Bob](https://alice-bob.com/newsroom/alice-bob-decode-ldpc-cat-codes/) has integrated the [NVIDIA NVQLink](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/quantum-computing/nvqlink/) platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities.
[Quandela](https://www.quandela.com/about-us/newsroom/gpu-qpu-integration-nvidia-nvqlink/) has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a [DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/) system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications.

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
body:
Get the developer newsletter
Product updates, how-tos, community spotlights, and more. Delivered monthly to your inbox.
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.
In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.
Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.
Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.
As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.
Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?
With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s [Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_(source_control_system)) and Meta’s [Sapling](https://sapling-scm.com/), so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:
Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.
Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.
A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.
Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.
Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.
The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.
It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.
In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,[1](#footnote-1) along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.
This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.
A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.
This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.
A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.
Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.
Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.
In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same n

title: Mix, Don't Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings
body:
For most languages of the world, language model pre-training operates in a data-constrained regime where models must repeat their training data many times, degrading generalization. Two remedies exist: aggressive hyperparameter tuning such as high weight decay, and mixing in data from a high-resource auxiliary language to directly aid the low-resource target. While hyperparameter tuning regularizes the model by shrinking weights to restrict network capacity, auxiliary data mixing uses a tunable mixing ratio to expand the training distribution and diversify the training signal with new knowledge. Both offer a principled way to improve training in a data-constrained domain. We compare these levers systematically across four model scales from 150M to 1.43B parameters, using Arabic as the low-resource target and English as the auxiliary, over approximately 1000 pre-training runs. Three findings emerge. First, mixing yields larger improvements than hyperparameter tuning on both validation loss and downstream task accuracy, and the gap grows with model size. Second, we quantify how much mixing helps: it boosts performance by an amount equivalent to 2â3Ã the unique target data on validation loss and 2â13Ã on downstream task accuracy, with the gain scaling steeply with model size. Third, this divergence reveals that target-language validation loss systematically underestimates mixingâs value. Mixing regularizes by diversifying the training signal and contributes knowledge the repeated target corpus cannot supply; validation loss captures only the first effect. Our practical recommendations are: mix in a high-resource language, prioritize the mixing ratio over hyperparameter tuning, and transfer hyperparameters from a small proxy model via Î¼P.

title: Uber's CISO on building an insider threat program for AI
body:
Uber's CISO on building an insider threat program for AI
Uber's CISO, Philip Martin, on the importance of monitoring and observability for AI agents, and how Uber's open-source tooling works alongside Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.
Uber runs one of the world's largest real-time marketplaces, with over 40 million trips and delivery orders a day. Philip Martin, Uber's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), leads the team that protects Uber's data and the riders, drivers, and couriers who use the platform in the real world. His team started working with Claude on threat modeling before Claude Code existed, assembling context by hand. Now, with Claude Fable, Claude gathers that context itself from code, design docs, and ticket history.
Martin thinks AI agents need the same kind of insider threat program companies already run for their employees. We spoke with him about that idea, why he thinks so much about accidental misuse, and how Uber's open-source monitoring tools work alongside Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.
How are frontier models changing your security team’s work?
The really big difference between prior models and today’s frontier models is their ability to incorporate additional context over long time horizons, and as a result, generate really specific outputs. When we're doing security reviews or threat modeling for a given service application, we can let the models consume a lot more context about the service, whether that's the code itself, design documents, issues in Jira, or historical context on what the service is supposed to do and what it interacts with.
I see the same thing emerging with teams of agents. I can imagine a world in the not-too-distant future where each service has an agent associated with it that understands that service very well, and those agents can talk to each other, the same way the services might in production, about the threat model: this is my threat model, this is where my data comes from. That team-of-agents effect will take us to the next level of efficacy.
Uber worked with our team Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. Why was this important for Uber?
One thing Anthropic and Uber have in common is a bone-deep focus on safety, albeit in very different contexts. When Uber thinks about safety, we think about rider safety, protecting personal data. Anthropic wants to prevent the misuse of its frontier models, but Uber needs to protect our customer data, our trade secrets, and any other proprietary information. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards allow us to strike this balance: the safeguards are in place, but our data is not accessible to Anthropic without our permission.
It gives us control of our data and control of the risk mitigation and the actions we decide to take after a safeguard is triggered. I think we share a responsibility to make sure these models are used safely and effectively in the world.
When your team walked us through the design, it was clear that you heard our feedback. You put us in the driver's seat. This allows us to protect our data while still being responsible stewards of the capabilities of these models.
How Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fit with the safety monitoring you already run on AI deployments Uber?
We've done a ton of work since the very beginning on how we deploy AI safely within Uber. We recently open-sourced a product called [AI Detection and Response (ADR) (opens in new tab)](https://github.com/uber/ADR), designed to gather real-time telemetry and take real-time action in the agent harnesses we deploy.
It complements Anthropic's safeguards, because we now have access to enhanced data to detect when an agent is acting outside its bounds and respond in real time. We have our own view of what's going on, plus output from Anthropic's classifier, and we can integrate both into our overall detection environment, much like a traditional cybersecurity one. It's all about assembling context effectively to reach a decision as fast, and with as much certainty, as possible.
I think we'll see Enterprise Frontier Safeguards feed into ADR as a data source. Together with our LLM gateway, which builds a perimeter and controls how AI is used within Uber, those make up our overall AI security architecture.
Where do you think defenders should prioritize their focus next when it comes to securing AI systems?
Number one is real-time detection and intervention: getting as close as we can to the human entering a prompt in a harness, to be able to tell them, "You probably don't want to do that," or "The tool this model is about to call, the place it's about to connect to, is probably not something you want to happen."
Number two is better understanding emerging patterns. We look at trends in model behavior and detect new behaviors we didn't know were possible. That becomes a cycle. We look at the data, in many cases with the assistance of LLMs, discover these behaviors as they appear, and build safeguards against them back into the real-time platform. Then new behaviors emerge, because constraints create new behaviors, and we find those too.
What would you tell other leaders who are hesitant about the monitoring frontier models require?
AI adoption is a business imperative. It's coming whether we want it or not, and it's going to bring real benefits to businesses and people around the world. But there's also real potential for harm, and the stakes rise as models get more capable and take on more complex, autonomous work.
Every company already runs an insider threat program for its people. Nobody argues about that. We accept the sometimes onerous data retention, and we monitor things we'd rather not monitor, because we know humans occasionally act outside the bounds of their role, for any number of reasons.
Frontier models introduce the same risk. These models may be directed to act outside the constraints we expect them to operate within. So we need the equivalent capability for AI. That insider threat program for models is going to be essential to rolling these systems out safely and securely.
Learn more about [Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/enterprise-frontier-safeguards).

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
body:
Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
12th October 2026
Python 3.15 [is here](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3150/)! Here’s the essential [What’s new in Python 3.15](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.
First, some highlights from Python 3.15.
Explicit lazy imports
I’m most excited about [Explicit lazy imports](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#pep-810-explicit-lazy-imports) from [PEP 810](https://peps.python.org/pep-0810/). These let you import modules like so:
lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path
The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.
My [LLM](https://llm.datasette.io/) CLI tool implements plugins. I had to [recommend manual lazy imports](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/plugins/advanced-model-plugins.html#tip-lazily-load-expensive-dependencies) in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers
could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm
command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.
Unpacking in comprehensions
The new [*sublist for sublist in lists]
unpacking syntax is neat. Here’s an illustration [lifted from the documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#pep-798-unpacking-in-comprehensions):
lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]] [*L for L in lists] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}] {*s for s in sets} # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}] {**d for d in dicts} # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}
[PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions](https://peps.python.org/pep-0798/) by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax [from PEP 448](https://peps.python.org/pep-0448/), which landed [in Python 3.5](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.5.html#pep-448-additional-unpacking-generalizations) back in 2015.
A sampling profiler
Python’s existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile
to [profiling.tracing](https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/profiling.tracing.html#module-profiling.tracing), and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka [profiling.sampling](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#tachyon-high-frequency-statistical-sampling-profiler).
Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They’re very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.
I’ve [previously used tools](https://simonwillison.net/tags/profiling/) like [py-spy](https://github.com/benfred/py-spy) for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.
If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo
on macOS):
sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234
Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:
It can also produce [flame graphs like this](https://simonw.github.io/research/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/artifacts/flamegraph.html) and [heat maps like this](https://simonw.github.io/research/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/artifacts/heatmap/index.html), and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.
3.15 isn’t much faster than 3.14
Miguel Grinberg investigated [How fast is Python 3.15?](https://blog.miguelgrinberg.com/post/how-fast-is-python-3-15) the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.
Miguel’s [explorations of 3.14](https://blog.miguelgrinberg.com/post/python-3-14-is-here-how-fast-is-it) last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.
Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv
I used the following sequence of commands to get uv
to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv
itself to ensure it knew about the new release:
uv self update
Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:
uv python install 3.15
And told uv
that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run
command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:
uv python pin --global 3.15
Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:
uv run python --version
I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install
. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:
uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15
Then I can confirm the version like this:
datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq
Highlights from Python 3.11
The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially [no longer supported](https://devguide.python.org/versions/).
My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.
Here’s the [What’s new in Python 3.11](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html) document. I finally get to rely on [tomllib](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tomllib.html#module-tomllib) being available!
Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio
. 3.11 adds [TaskGroup](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.TaskGroup) and [timeout()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.timeout), and [several more](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html#asyncio) new features.
datetime.UTC
is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc
.
Python’s SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:
-
[setlimit()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.setlimit)and[getlimit()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.getlimit)expose a mechanism for setting[SQLite runtime limits](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/c_limit_attached.html)from Python. -
[create_window_function()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.create_window_function)lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class withstep()
,value()
,inverse()
, andfinalize()
methods. -
[blobopen()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.blobopen)provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of largeBLOB
binary values stored in a SQLite row. - You can now call
set_authorizer(None)
to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!
Plus a whole bunch of [improvements to Python’s typing system](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html#new-feat-related-type-hints-311).
I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here’s [my first Datasette PR](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/pull/2998) removing that set_authorizer(None)
workaround.
I’ve also updated my [click-app](https://github.com/simonw/click-app), [datasette-plugin](https://github.com/simonw/datasette-plugin), [python-lib](https://github.com/simonw/python-lib), and [llm-plugin](https://github.com/simonw/llm-plugin) cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
body:
More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers.

Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review.

title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual
body:
“Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries.

The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming.

- https://www.linkedin.com/in/hackintoshrao/

title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
body:
A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse.

An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers.

title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
body:
As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably.
At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure.
NVIDIA contributed key [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open [NVIDIA MGX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/mgx/) architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure.
Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing.
NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances
At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements:
- NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience.
- NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory.
- Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations.
- Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era.
- NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics.
- NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs.
Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide.
The [news at OCP](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/ocp-summit/) spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance.
Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#mgx)
NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative.
Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale.
For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs.
MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse.
The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the [NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time.
Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories.
NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#dsx)
[NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx/) applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale.
At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal:
[NVIDIA Config Manager](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nv-config-manager): Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/[NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cluster-readiness-engine): Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins[NVIDIA Rack Management Service](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nv-rms): Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management.[Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/cluster-api-provider-nico): Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days.
Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms.
Developers can visit the [DSX AI Factory Github page](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform.
NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#open-standards)
For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on.
At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta to publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The [Open Data Center Specification v0.7](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/open-data-center-spec-revision-0-7-0-4-pdf) defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout.
The [OCP Grid Resilience Specification](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-base-spec-interface-specification-between-hyperscalers-and-utility-grid-for-disturbance-performance-pdf), published by Google, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds.
With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers.
Being [NVIDIA DSX reference design](https://docs.nvidia.com/dsx)-compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. For operators building Vera Rubin AI factories, there’s now a straight line from open community standard to a running system.
Visionbay.ai Designs 800VDC AI Factory for the Vera Rubin Era [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#visionbay)
As AI factories grow larger and more powerful, one challenge looms over them all: delivering enough power to the accelerated computing systems driving the next generation of AI.
At OCP, Visionbay unveiled plans for K-1, a next-generation AI factory platform designed around an [800 VDC architecture](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/800-vdc-power-architecture-ai-factory) and built with future NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments in mind. The project combines NVIDIA’s 800 VDC reference architecture with power and thermal technologies from Vertiv to create a scalable foundation for high-density AI infrastructure.
The design addresses a growing industry challenge. As AI training, inference and reasoning workloads expand, rack power densities continue to rise. Traditional low-voltage power distribution becomes increasingly difficult to scale, requiring more copper, more cabling and more power-conversion equipment.
By adopting NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture, K-1 creates a path toward higher-density AI infrastructure while preserving flexibility for existing deployments. Rather than requiring a complete transition on day one, the platform is designed to phase in 800 VDC distribution where it delivers the greatest benefit, helping operators prepare for future generations of accelerated computing without extensive facility redesign.
The architecture is designed around cluster-level power centers that centralize AC-to-DC conversion and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources. The approach simplifies downstream power delivery, supports modular expansion and creates repeatable building blocks for future AI factory growth.
K-1 also reflects the system-level design philosophy behind NVIDIA AI factories, where power, cooling and computing are engineered together. With support for liquid-cooled infrastructure, scalable power distribution and future Vera Rubin-class deployments, the project demonstrates how ecosystem partners are translating NVIDIA’s AI factory architecture into deployable infrastructure designed for the next era of accelerated computing.
Meta and NVIDIA Advance AI Networking With Spectrum-6 and Multiplane Technology [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#meta)
At the event, Meta and NVIDIA announced that Meta is adopting NVIDIA Spectrum-6 102.4Tb/s Ethernet switches to build larger, higher-performance NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories on open networking.
Spectrum-6 delivers twice the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4, and provides a lossless Ethernet AI fabric at 200G per lane, with high effective bandwidth and performance isolation that keeps one job’s traffic from slowing another’s.
Meta’s Spectrum-6-based switch, N-IceCube, slots into IcePack, Meta’s 100T, liquid-cooled rack. N-IceCube runs the Facebook Open Switching System (FBOSS), Meta’s open source network operating system that contributed to OCP to support efficient networking at hyperscale.
FBOSS is built on the Switch Abstraction Interface, an OCP standard NVIDIA helped develop, providing a vendor-independent way of controlling switch hardware. Together, these technologies support agentic AI factories of more than 100,000 GPUs that train and serve massive [mixture-of-experts](ht

title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
body:
A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work.

Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings.

title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
body:
Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU.

The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself.

title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
body:
An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve.

Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct.

title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
body:
While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop.

Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment.

title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
body:
Two AI interns. One handles 96% of conversations alone, the other only 80%. The dashboard picks the wrong one.

Druid AI's team, including co-founder and chief product officer Dan Bălăceanu, shows why containment rate, the metric on every agent dashboard, can point you to the wrong agent. In their bank example, the intern who escalated more often was handing senior bankers customers who were about to refinance. They walk through a performance review framework built with their customers: seven pillars split into what the agent is configured with and what it does at runtime, with governance across both. Twenty-six components are each scored 0, 1 or 2 (missing, defined, or actually governed and tracked over time) and weighted by business impact, with governance and mandate weighted highest. They cover error tolerance, risk, compliance, observability, drift, hallucination, tone and sentiment, the agent's mandate, scope, business case and budget, a shared platform, and validating outcomes. They also show a dashboard that stays green all year while the agent's real score slides from 83% to 60%, how to answer the ROI question, and why containment targets differ by industry in Druid's 2026 AI Adoption Benchmark.

In this talk:
• Why containment rate can reward the wrong agent
• A seven-pillar scorecard: configuration, runtime and governance
• Scoring and weighting 26 components by business impact
• Answering ROI and setting industry-specific targets
